On October 26, 2016, two weeks before the presidential election, Comey learned that FBI agents investigating an unrelated case involving former congressman Anthony Weiner had discovered emails on Weiner's computer between his wife, Huma Abedin, and Clinton.

Claiming he believed it would take months to review Weiner's emails, Comey decided he had to inform Congress that the investigation was being reopened due to new information.[7] Justice Department lawyers warned him that giving out public information about an investigation was inconsistent with department policy, but he considered the policy to be "guidance" rather than an ironclad rule.[120] He decided that to not reveal the new information would be misleading to Congress and the public.[121] On October 28, Comey sent a letter to members of Congress advising them that the FBI was reviewing more emails.

Members of Congress revealed the information to the public within minutes.[122] Republican and Democratic lawmakers, as well as the Clinton and Trump campaigns, called on Comey to provide additional details.

By May 11, however, in a direct contradiction of the earlier statements by the White House, Vice President Mike Pence, and the contents of the dismissal letter itself, President Trump stated to Lester Holt in an NBC News interview that Comey's dismissal was in fact "my decision" and "I was going to fire [Comey] regardless of recommendation [by Jeff Sessions and Rod Rosenstein]."[188][189] Trump later said of the dismissal "when I decided to just do it [fire Comey], I said to myself, I said 'You know, this Russia thing with Trump and Russia is a made-up story.'"[190] In the same televised interview, Trump labelled Comey "a showboat" and "grandstander".
In 2020, Comey's tenure as the FBI director has been depicted in the _Showtime_ TV mini-series _The Comey Rule_; he was portrayed by Jeff Daniels.
